COT on commodities covering managed money accounts in the week to 13 October saw broad selling extend into a second consecutive week despite another period of overall index strength, which lifted the Bloomberg Commodity Index (BCOM) by 1.5%. However, as the table highlights, gains were primarily driven by energy, while all other sectors suffered setbacks, led by grains and precious metals. The reporting period ended just ahead of last Wednesday’s US CPI release, which subsequently triggered considerable turbulence across financial markets.

Managed money buying was concentrated in Brent crude, which gained 5% during the week, followed by gasoil and natural gas, while the speculative net long in sugar rose to a five-year high.

All metals saw net selling, led by gold ahead of the US CPI release. However, the bulk of the selling was once again concentrated in grains, where a fourth consecutive week of long liquidation followed last month’s record net long of more than one million contracts. Corn suffered the largest reduction as traders responded to the latest and particularly bearish USDA WASDE report, which triggered the biggest one-day corn price slump since 2023.

COT on forex – week to 13 October: Dollar longs surge as positioning once again becomes increasingly stretched

The rapid rebuilding of long dollar positions extended into a fourth consecutive week, supported by continued, albeit relatively modest, dollar strength ahead of last Wednesday’s US CPI release. Dollar strength was particularly pronounced against the euro, amid ongoing political and fiscal turmoil in Europe, and the Mexican peso, which fell to its lowest level of the year after minutes from the latest central bank meeting suggested policymakers were increasingly open to rate cuts, undermining the currency’s carry appeal.

Overall, the gross dollar long against eight IMM currency futures surged 27% to USD 44.6 billion, an 11-week high and a remarkable USD 37 billion increase over the past four weeks. The euro net short reached a ten-year high of 138,000 contracts, equivalent to USD 19.3 billion, while the sterling short climbed to a nine-year high of 107,000 contracts, or USD 9 billion. Meanwhile, the Australian dollar short reached an all-time record of 117,000 contracts, equivalent to USD 8.2 billion, a remarkable turnaround from a 13-year high at 86k contracts recorded back in May.

These increasingly stretched positions highlight the extent to which speculative investors have embraced the dollar's recovery. However, they also point to a potentially vulnerable and increasingly one-sided trade, with the risk of a sharp reversal should the fundamental or technical backdrop shift. The rapid unwinding of dollar longs following the multi-year positioning peak in late July serves as a timely reminder of how quickly sentiment can turn when too many investors find themselves on the same side of the trade.
